body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Tiered drug interaction alerts and prescriber response: a cluster randomised trial on 24 wards","authors":"Halvorsen-Ibe K, Castaneda-Wright P, Mbeki-Sundqvist L","year":2020,"venue":"Journal of Clinical Decision Support","doi":"10.5555/jcds.2020.0127","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"We randomised 24 wards in two hospitals to a tiered drug interaction alert display or the standard display for six months. With tiering, 29 percent of high-severity interruptive alerts were accepted, compared with 11 percent under the standard display. The number of interruptive alerts per 100 orders fell from 8.2 to 1.9. Pharmacist review found no increase in dispensed moderate-interaction combinations judged harmful. Prescribers rotated between wards, which may have diluted the difference, and adverse drug events were not measured directly."},{"title":"Alert override rates in electronic prescribing: a multi-site analysis","authors":"Okafor-Lindberg S, Petit-Achterberg R","year":2016,"venue":"Health Informatics Practice","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Across 9 hospitals, 1.2 million drug interaction alerts were analysed. Override rates were between 90 and 96 percent at every site. High-severity alerts were overridden almost as often as low-severity ones. Override rates rose with the number of alerts a prescriber saw per shift. Reasons were documented for fewer than a third of overrides, and documented reasons were often free text that did not name the interaction. The authors describe alert volume as the main driver of override behaviour. Sites with the highest alert volume also had the highest override rates."},{"title":"Interventions to reduce alert fatigue in computerised prescribing: a systematic review","authors":"Nakashima-Dube T, Ferreira-Olsen A, Varga-Mwangi B, Sato-Holm C","year":2023,"venue":"Digital Health Evidence Reviews","doi":"10.5555/dher.2023.0056","providerType":"review","abstract":"We included 27 studies of tiering, suppression of low-value alerts, redesign of alert text and prescriber-specific filtering. Tiering and suppression reduced alert volume in every study that reported it, and acceptance of the remaining alerts rose in most. Only 4 studies measured patient outcomes, and none found a clear change in adverse drug events. Most studies were before-and-after designs with concurrent changes to prescribing systems. Two randomised studies reported contamination between arms because prescribers worked across units. Few studies reported how long prescribers spent reading alerts."},{"title":"Appropriateness of overrides as an outcome in alert trials: a pharmacist review of 1,000 overridden alerts","authors":"Lindqvist-Obi M, Adeyemi-Carter J","year":2021,"venue":"Medication Safety Methods","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Two pharmacists independently reviewed 1,000 overridden drug interaction alerts using a written definition of an appropriate override. They judged 87 percent of overrides appropriate, with good agreement (kappa 0.71). Override rates alone misclassified many appropriate overrides as failures and missed inappropriate acceptances. Review took about four minutes per alert. Agreement was lowest for overrides justified by monitoring plans that were not documented in the record. We recommend an outcome that combines accepted alerts and overrides judged appropriate, measured on a random sample when volumes are large."},{"title":"Contamination in randomised trials of prescribing decision support when prescribers rotate","authors":"Brennan-Osei D, Tanaka-Lund F, Reid-Okonkwo G","year":2019,"venue":"Trials in Health Informatics","doi":"10.5555/thi.2019.0033","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Using rotation data from 3 hospitals, we simulated trials of a prescribing alert display. When displays were set by ward but prescribers were randomised, 40 percent of orders were exposed to the other arm. Randomising wards reduced exposure to the other arm to under 10 percent but needed a design effect of about 2.1 for the same number of orders. Stratifying by specialty reduced imbalance when there were fewer than 40 wards. We recommend ward-level randomisation whenever the display is a ward setting."},{"title":"Harm from suppressed moderate interaction alerts: pharmacist surveillance after tiering","authors":"Dubois-Achebe H, Quist-Moreno V","year":2025,"venue":"Medication Safety Methods","doi":"10.5555/msm.2025.0018","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"After tiering in one hospital, pharmacists reviewed 2,400 dispensed moderate-interaction combinations over four months. They judged 14 as having caused or contributed to harm (0.6 percent), a rate similar to the year before tiering. Most harms involved potassium-raising combinations in older adults with kidney impairment. The surveillance took about 6 pharmacist hours a week. No harm was judged to have followed a combination that remained interruptive. The authors suggest targeting surveillance at a short list of combinations that caused most harm rather than reviewing every moderate interaction."},{"title":"Why prescribers override interaction alerts: a questionnaire study in teaching hospitals","authors":"Achterberg-Moss E, Oduya-Fischer R","year":2018,"venue":"Health Informatics Practice","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Among 410 prescribers in three teaching hospitals who answered a questionnaire, 72 percent said they overrode interaction alerts without reading them at least weekly. The most common reasons given were that the interaction was already known, that the alert appeared for combinations used routinely, and that the alert text was too long. Junior doctors reported more alerts per shift than consultants. Prescribers supported tiering if high-severity alerts stayed interruptive and were fewer. Consultants were more likely than junior doctors to say that an alert had changed one of their prescriptions in the past month."}]}
